title: Diverse approaches to diverse receptors: a multidimensional study of caffeine perception
content: Humans exhibit striking, heritable variability in bitter taste sensitivity that has spurred genetics research for 95 years (Wooding 2006). It was first discovered in the early 1930s that individuals vary profoundly in ability to perceive phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) and its chemical relatives, with some people able to sense it at millimolar concentrations while others find it tasteless. Further, the trait segregated strongly in families, revealing its genetic basis. Research in subsequent decades demonstrated that variability in bitter perception is not restricted to PTC; it extends to myriad small molecules, including many found in the human diet (Reed and Knaapila 2010). Moreover, it predicts eating behaviors and their downstream consequences for health, such as preferences for vegetables and predispositions to obesity (Dinehart et al. 2006; Feeney et al. 2011). These discoveries galvanized efforts to uncover the functional basis of variability in bitter perception, driving the development of diverse approaches to the problem. They have come to include population genetic studies aimed at identifying new mutations, tests for correlations between genetic variants and perception, in vitro assays of mechanistic processes in cells, computational analyses of structure, and others. In this volume of Chemical Senses, Numabe et al. (2025) unify these in a multifaceted study of genetic variation in the perception of an especially interesting compound, caffeine.
